2. Temperature: Higher temperature gives particles more kinetic energy to break free.

beats.narration: Hello! Quick question before we begin.
When you hang a wet school shirt out in the balcony after washing, the water completely disappears after an hour or two. Where did that water go?

ask.question: Where does the water from wet clothes go, even though the balcony never reaches 100°C?
ask.expect: The water turns into water vapour and mixes into the air at room temperature without boiling.
ask.hint: Think about what state water changes into when it leaves the fabric into the surrounding air.

beats.narration: Exactly. The water turns into vapour and escapes into the air.
Water boils at a hundred degrees Celsius, but your balcony is barely thirty degrees. Yet the liquid still changes into vapour.
This phenomenon of a liquid changing into vapour at any temperature below its boiling point is called evaporation.
Let us look right inside the liquid to see why this happens.
In any liquid, particles are constantly moving and colliding. They do not all have the exact same kinetic energy.
A small fraction of particles at the surface happens to have higher kinetic energy than those deep inside.
Because they have higher energy, they can break free from the attractive forces of surrounding particles and fly off into the air.
So is evaporation happening throughout the entire liquid, or only at the top boundary?

ask.question: Why is evaporation called a 'surface phenomenon' while boiling is a 'bulk phenomenon'?
ask.expect: Because only particles at the surface escape in evaporation, whereas in boiling particles throughout the bulk liquid gain enough energy to form vapour.
ask.hint: Look at where the escaping particles are sitting in our diagram.

beats.narration: You already use the rules of evaporation every single day without realising it.
When you put clothes out to dry, you spread them wide instead of leaving them folded. Why?
More surface means more particles sitting at the boundary ready to jump out.
On a hot sunny day, clothes dry much faster than on a cold morning. That is temperature.
Now think about a rainy day in July. Why do clothes take so long to dry during the monsoon?

ask.question: Why does high humidity slow down the rate of evaporation?
ask.expect: Because the air already holds a large amount of water vapour, so it cannot easily take in more.
ask.hint: Humidity means how much water vapour is already present in the air.

beats.narration: And finally, if clothes are not drying, we turn on a ceiling fan.
Here is an experiment you can test right now. If you pour a drop of hand sanitiser or acetone onto your palm, your hand immediately feels icy cold.
Why does that happen?

ask.question: Where does the evaporating liquid get the energy it needs to change into vapour from your palm?
ask.expect: It absorbs heat energy directly from your skin and palm, causing your palm to lose heat and feel cool.
ask.hint: Think about what surface the liquid is resting on and what energy it takes from it.

beats.narration: When the fastest particles escape from the liquid, they absorb heat energy from your palm and surroundings to turn into vapour.
Because heat is taken away from your skin, the temperature of your palm drops.
The same exact principle keeps water cold in a clay matka during hot Indian summers.
So whenever a liquid evaporates, it takes heat away with it. That is why evaporation always cools things down!
